title: Using the Earth's resources and sustainable development

notes.definition: Humans use the Earth's resources to provide warmth, shelter, food and transport. Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
explanation: Everything we use comes from the Earth's resources: the land, the oceans and the atmosphere. We use these resources to provide warmth (fuels for heating), shelter (building materials such as wood, stone, metals and glass), food (crops and animals) and transport (fuels, and materials for vehicles and roads). Natural resources such as timber, cotton, wool and rubber come from plants and animals, and these are often supplemented or replaced by products of agriculture and by synthetic products made by chemists.

Resources can be described as finite or renewable. A finite resource is one that is used up much faster than it can be replaced, so it will eventually run out. Examples include crude oil, natural gas, coal and metal ores. A renewable resource is one that can be replaced at the same rate as (or faster than) it is used, for example wood from managed forests, cotton, wool and biofuels made from crops. In the exam you may be given information about a resource and asked to decide whether it is finite or renewable.

Chemistry has an important role in making our use of resources more sustainable. Chemists develop new materials (for example synthetic polymers that replace natural rubber or wool), improve agricultural processes (for example making fertilisers so that more food can be grown on the same land) and improve industrial processes so that they use less energy, produce less waste and make better use of raw materials.

Sustainable development means meeting our needs today in a way that does not stop people in the future from meeting their needs. In practice this involves using less of finite resources, choosing renewable resources where possible, reusing and recycling materials, reducing waste and pollution, and using processes that need less energy (for example using catalysts so reactions run at lower temperatures).

You should be able to interpret and evaluate information about resources: for example, using data on reserves and rate of use to estimate how long a resource will last, comparing a natural product with a synthetic one, or judging whether a proposed process is sustainable. Good evaluations consider the supply of raw materials, energy use, waste products and environmental impact, and finish with a justified conclusion.
keyFacts: We use the Earth's resources for warmth, shelter, food and transport.
Natural resources are supplemented, and sometimes replaced, by agricultural and synthetic products.
Finite resources (crude oil, natural gas, coal, metal ores) will run out because they form far more slowly than we use them.
Renewable resources (timber, cotton, wool, crops for biofuels) can be replaced as fast as they are used.
Sustainable development meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
Chemistry improves agricultural and industrial processes to provide new products and to support sustainable development.
Catalysts help sustainability by lowering the energy needed for industrial processes.
Years a resource will last can be estimated as reserves ÷ rate of use (assuming use stays constant).

keyTerms.definition: A resource that is used up faster than it is replaced, so it will eventually run out (for example crude oil or metal ores).
A resource that can be replaced at the same rate as, or faster than, it is used (for example timber from managed forests).
Development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
A material obtained directly from the Earth, plants or animals, such as wood, cotton, wool or rubber.
A material made by chemical processes to supplement or replace a natural product, such as poly(ethene) or nylon.
The amount of a resource that is known to exist and can be extracted economically.

equations.name: Estimated lifetime of a resource
equations.formula: years remaining = known reserves ÷ amount used per year
equations.units: years (reserves and use must be in the same units)

workedExamples.title: How long will a reserve last?
workedExamples.question: The known reserves of a metal ore are 7.2 billion tonnes. The ore is mined at 0.16 billion tonnes per year. Estimate how many years the reserves will last, and give one reason why the real answer may be different.
steps: Years remaining = reserves ÷ rate of use.
The estimate assumes use stays constant and no new reserves are found.
workedExamples.answer: About 45 years. It may be shorter if demand increases, or longer if new reserves are discovered, recycling increases or extraction of lower-grade ores becomes economic.

workedExamples.title: Finite or renewable?
workedExamples.question: A company makes a fuel from oilseed rape. The crop grows in one year. Another company makes a fuel from crude oil, which formed over millions of years. Classify each fuel as finite or renewable and explain your answer.
steps: Compare the rate of formation with the rate of use.
Oilseed rape can be regrown every year, as fast as it is used.
Crude oil took millions of years to form, much slower than we use it.
workedExamples.answer: The oilseed rape fuel is renewable because the crop is replaced each year; the crude oil fuel is finite because it is used much faster than it forms.

workedExamples.title: Percentage of a resource from a renewable source
workedExamples.question: A country used 250 TWh of electricity in a year. 85 TWh came from renewable sources. Calculate the percentage from renewable sources.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think renewable means the resource can never run out however much we use.
misconceptions.right: In fact a renewable resource only stays available if it is used no faster than it is replaced; overfelling a forest can still use timber up.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think sustainable development means stopping all use of finite resources.
misconceptions.right: In fact it means meeting today's needs without compromising future generations, for example by using finite resources efficiently, recycling and switching to renewables where possible.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think synthetic products are always less sustainable than natural ones.
misconceptions.right: In fact it depends on the raw materials, energy and waste involved; a synthetic product can reduce pressure on land or animals, but many are made from finite crude oil.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that 'reserves ÷ use' gives an exact date the resource will run out.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is only an estimate: use changes, new reserves are found and recycling changes demand.

realWorld: Synthetic fibres such as nylon and polyester supplement natural wool and cotton in clothing, reducing the land needed for sheep and cotton crops.
Fertilisers made by the chemical industry allow farmers to grow much more food on the same area of land.
Timber certification schemes check that wood comes from forests replanted as fast as trees are felled, keeping timber a renewable resource.
examTips: Learn the definition of sustainable development word for word: 'meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'.
When classifying a resource, compare how fast it is replaced with how fast it is used; that is the deciding idea, not whether it is natural.
In 'evaluate' questions give points on both sides (for example raw materials, energy, waste, cost) and finish with a justified conclusion.
When estimating how long a resource will last, check the units of reserves and rate of use match before dividing.
summary: Earth's resources provide warmth, shelter, food and transport.
Natural resources are supplemented by agricultural and synthetic products.
Finite resources run out; renewable resources are replaced as fast as they are used.
Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising future generations.
Chemistry improves processes and products to support sustainable development.
Years remaining ≈ reserves ÷ annual use, which is only an estimate.

One used up much faster than it is replaced, so it will run out, e.g. crude oil, coal, metal ores.
One that can be replaced at the same rate as it is used, e.g. timber, cotton, wool, crops.

flashcards.front: Give two examples of natural products that are supplemented by synthetic ones
flashcards.back: Wool and cotton (by polyester and nylon); natural rubber (by synthetic rubber).

flashcards.front: How does chemistry help sustainable development?
flashcards.back: By improving agricultural and industrial processes, providing new products, and reducing energy use and waste.

flashcards.front: How do catalysts make a process more sustainable?
flashcards.back: They lower the temperature (energy) needed, saving fuel.

flashcards.front: How can you estimate how long a resource will last?
flashcards.back: Divide known reserves by the amount used per year (same units).

flashcards.front: Is crude oil finite or renewable?
flashcards.back: Finite: it formed over millions of years and is used much faster.

flashcards.front: Why is wood from managed forests renewable?
flashcards.back: New trees are planted to replace those felled, so it is replaced as fast as it is used.
Crude oil, natural gas, coal, metal ores (any three).

flashcards.front: Why are estimates of resource lifetimes uncertain?
flashcards.back: Rate of use changes, new reserves are discovered, and recycling and new technology change demand.

questions.question: Which of these is a finite resource?
options: Wool
Timber from a managed forest
Natural gas
Cotton
markScheme: 1 mark: Natural gas
questions.explanation: Natural gas formed over millions of years and is used far faster than it forms, so it will run out. Wool, cotton and managed timber can be replaced each year or so.

questions.question: Which statement is the definition of sustainable development?
options: Development that uses only renewable resources
Development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Development that produces no waste at all
Development that uses the cheapest raw materials available
markScheme: 1 mark: meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
questions.explanation: This is the AQA definition. Using only renewables or producing no waste may help, but they are not the definition.

questions.question: Humans use the Earth's resources to provide warmth, shelter, food and which other need?
options: Transport
Entertainment
Education
Medicine
markScheme: 1 mark: Transport
questions.explanation: The specification lists warmth, shelter, food and transport as the basic uses of Earth's resources.

questions.question: Which of these is a synthetic product that can replace a natural one?
options: Cotton
Wool
Silk
Nylon
markScheme: 1 mark: Nylon
questions.explanation: Nylon is made by chemical processes and can replace natural fibres such as silk or wool. Cotton, wool and silk are natural products.

questions.question: Which feature decides whether a resource is renewable?
options: Whether it comes from a living thing
Whether it is cheap to extract
Whether it can be replaced at the same rate as it is used
Whether it is found in the atmosphere
markScheme: 1 mark: whether it can be replaced at the same rate as it is used
questions.explanation: The key idea is the rate of replacement compared with the rate of use. Coal came from living things but is finite because it forms too slowly.

questions.question: Coal formed from the remains of plants. Why is coal classed as a finite resource?
options: It cannot be burned more than once
It took millions of years to form and is used much faster than it forms
It is found only in a few countries
It releases carbon dioxide when it burns
markScheme: 1 mark: it formed over millions of years and is used much faster than it forms
questions.explanation: Being made from plants does not make a resource renewable; the formation rate is far too slow compared with the rate we use it.

questions.question: Which change to an industrial process would make it more sustainable?
options: Using a higher temperature so that the reaction is faster
Using a catalyst so the process runs at a lower temperature
Using a finite raw material instead of a renewable one
Sending the by-products to landfill
markScheme: 1 mark: using a catalyst so the process runs at a lower temperature
questions.explanation: A catalyst allows lower temperatures, so less fuel is burned. Higher temperatures use more energy, and landfill wastes materials.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows information about a resource.
A scientist estimates that the known reserves will last 30 years.
Which statement about this estimate is correct?

headers: Known reserves in millions of tonnes
Use in millions of tonnes per year

options: The resource will definitely run out in exactly 30 years
The estimate assumes the rate of use stays the same and no new reserves are found
The estimate will be too long if recycling increases
The estimate is renewable because it is less than 100 years
markScheme: 1 mark: the estimate assumes constant use and no new reserves
questions.explanation: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 years only if use stays constant. Increased recycling would make the resource last longer, not shorter.

questions.question: A plastic bag can be made from crude oil or from starch grown in maize. Which statement is the best evaluation of sustainability?
options: The maize bag is fully sustainable because maize is natural
The crude oil bag is more sustainable because oil is cheaper
The maize raw material is renewable, but growing maize uses land, fertiliser and energy that must also be considered
Both are equally sustainable because both make bags
markScheme: 1 mark: maize is renewable but land, fertiliser and energy use must also be considered
questions.explanation: A good evaluation considers the whole picture. A renewable raw material helps, but farming has its own resource costs.

questions.question: Which of these is a renewable resource?
options: Copper ore
Crude oil
Coal
Wool
markScheme: 1 mark: Wool
questions.explanation: Sheep grow new wool every year, so wool is replaced as fast as it is used. Copper ore, crude oil and coal are finite.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows information about a metal ore.
Calculate how many years the known reserves will last if the rate of mining stays the same.

headers: Known reserves in millions of tonnes
Rate of mining in millions of tonnes per year

markScheme: 1 mark: 30 years
questions.explanation: Years remaining = reserves ÷ rate of use = 900 ÷ 30 = 30 years.

questions.question: State what is meant by a finite resource.
acceptedAnswers: used faster than it is replaced
cannot be replaced as fast as it is used
markScheme: 1 mark: a resource that will run out / is used faster than it can be replaced
questions.explanation: A finite resource forms much more slowly than we use it, so the supply is limited.

questions.question: Give two examples of finite resources.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: crude oil / natural gas / coal / a named metal ore
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels and metal ores are the standard examples of finite resources.

questions.question: Name two natural products that have been supplemented or replaced by synthetic products.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: wool / cotton / silk / rubber / wood / leather
questions.explanation: Synthetic fibres replace wool, cotton and silk; synthetic rubber replaces natural rubber; plastics replace wood in many uses.

questions.question: Explain why timber from a managed forest is described as a renewable resource.
acceptedAnswers: replaced as fast as it is used
new trees grow to replace felled trees
markScheme: 1 mark: new trees are planted to replace those cut down
1 mark: so timber is replaced at the same rate as it is used
questions.explanation: Renewable means the supply is replaced as fast as it is used, which managed replanting achieves.

questions.question: Describe two ways in which chemists contribute to sustainable development.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: developing catalysts so processes use less energy / making fertilisers to grow more food / developing new or synthetic materials to replace scarce natural ones / improving processes to reduce waste / developing recycling methods
questions.explanation: The specification says chemistry improves agricultural and industrial processes to provide new products and supports sustainable development.

questions.question: Biodiesel can be made from rapeseed oil. Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of using rapeseed oil rather than crude oil as a raw material for fuel.
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage: rapeseed is renewable / can be regrown each year
1 mark: disadvantage: uses farmland that could grow food / needs fertilisers and energy to grow and process
questions.explanation: Crops are renewable, but they compete with food for land and still need energy and fertilisers.

questions.question: A report estimates that reserves of a metal ore will last 40 years. Give three reasons why the metal may actually be available for longer than 40 years.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any three: new reserves discovered / more of the metal is recycled / new methods allow low-grade ores to be used / demand falls / other materials replace the metal
questions.explanation: The 40-year estimate assumes constant use and current reserves; any change that increases supply or reduces demand extends the lifetime.

questions.question: Explain why a resource that comes from living things can still be used in a way that is not sustainable.
markScheme: 1 mark: if it is used faster than it is replaced (for example forests felled without replanting)
1 mark: the resource would be depleted so future generations could not meet their needs
questions.explanation: Renewability depends on the balance between rate of use and rate of replacement, not only on the source.

questions.question: A student says: 'Recycling aluminium cans helps sustainable development.' Explain why the student is correct.
markScheme: 1 mark: reduces the amount of finite aluminium ore that must be mined / conserves the ore for future generations
1 mark: uses less energy than extracting new aluminium / reduces landfill waste
questions.explanation: Recycling conserves a finite resource and saves energy, so future generations are less disadvantaged.

questions.question:
Clothing can be made from cotton (a natural fibre grown as a crop) or from polyester (a synthetic fibre made from crude oil).
Compare the sustainability of the two fibres.
markScheme: Indicative content: cotton is renewable as it can be regrown each year; polyester is made from crude oil, a finite resource; cotton needs large areas of land, lots of water and often fertilisers and pesticides; polyester production uses energy from fossil fuels; polyester can be recycled; cotton is biodegradable.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear comparison of both fibres with points about raw material and at least one other factor (land, water, energy, disposal).
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or both fibres, for example cotton is renewable.
questions.explanation: Sustainability depends on more than whether the raw material is renewable: land, water, energy and disposal all matter.

questions.question:
A government wants industry to use the Earth's resources more sustainably.
Explain what is meant by sustainable development and evaluate ways in which chemistry can help industry and agriculture to become more sustainable.
markScheme: Indicative content: definition (meets needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs); finite resources such as crude oil and ores will run out; use renewable raw materials where possible; catalysts reduce energy use by lowering temperatures; recycling metals, glass and plastics conserves ores and energy; synthetic materials can supplement scarce natural ones; fertilisers increase crop yields so less land is needed, but excess fertiliser can pollute water; renewable raw materials may use land needed for food; reducing waste and finding uses for by-products.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct definition and a detailed, balanced evaluation of several methods, including at least one limitation, with a reasoned conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): definition or near definition and description of some methods with some explanation of why they help.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'recycle more' or 'use renewable resources'.
questions.explanation: Top answers define the term precisely and weigh benefits against limitations, for example fertilisers raise yields but may cause pollution.

questions.question:
A forest has 50 000 trees.
Each year 2500 trees are felled and 2500 new trees are planted.
Calculate the number of trees in the forest after 10 years.
questions.explanation: Felling equals replanting, so the number stays at 50 000: the timber is being used renewably.

questions.question: State one way in which humans use the Earth's resources to provide shelter.
markScheme: 1 mark: building materials such as wood, stone, bricks, metals, glass or concrete
questions.explanation: Shelter uses materials extracted from the Earth or grown, for example timber and stone.
